'''Summer savory''' (''Satureja hortensis'') is among the best known of the [[Satureja|savory]] genus. It is an annual, but otherwise is similar in use and flavor to the perennial [[winter savory]].  It is used more often than winter savory, which has a slightly more bitter flavor.

This [[herb]] has lilac tubular flowers which bloom in the northern hemisphere from July to September.
It grows to around {{convert|30|to|60|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} in height and has very slender, bronze-green leaves.

== Taxonomy ==
The species name ''Satureja hortensis'' was first published in 1753 by [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl von Linné]] in ''[[Species Plantarum]]'', Volume II (page 568).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Linné |first1=Carl von |url=https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/item/13830 |title=Caroli Linnaei ... Species plantarum :exhibentes plantas rite cognitas, ad genera relatas, cum differentiis specificis, nominibus trivialibus, synonymis selectis, locis natalibus, secundum systema sexuale digestas... |last2=Linné |first2=Carl von |last3=Salvius |first3=Lars |date=1753 |publisher=Impensis Laurentii Salvii |volume=2 |location=Holmiae}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=WFO Plant List {{!}} World Flora Online |url=https://wfoplantlist.org/taxon/wfo-0000304214-2023-12?page=1 |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=wfoplantlist.org}}</ref> [[Homotypic synonym]]s are ''Clinopodium hortense'' (L.) ([[Otto Kuntze|Kuntze]], 1891) and ''Thymus cunila'' [[Ernst Hans Ludwig Krause|(E.H.L.Krause]], 1903). [[Heterotypic synonym]]s are ''Clinopodium pachyphyllum'' ([[Karl Koch (botanist)|K.Koch]], Kuntze, 1891), ''Satureja altaica'' ([[Antonina Borissova|Boriss.]], 1953), ''Satureja brachiata'' ([[Jonathan Stokes|Stokes]], 1812), ''Satureja filicaulis'' ([[Heinrich Wilhelm Schott|Schott]] ex [[Pierre Edmond Boissier|Boiss.]], 1879), ''Satureja hortensis'' var. ''distans'' (K.Koch, 1849), ''Satureja laxiflora'' subsp. ''zuvandica'' (D.A.Kapan.<!--Q47119904-->, 1987), ''Satureja litwinowii'' ([[Johannes Theodor Schmalhausen|Schmalh.]] ex [[Vladimir Lipsky|Lipsky]], 1899), ''Satureja officinarum'' ([[Heinrich Johann Nepomuk von Crantz|Crantz]], 1766), ''Satureja pachyphylla'' (K.Koch, 1844), ''Satureja viminea'' ([[Nicolaas Laurens Burman|Burm.f.]], 1768) and ''Satureja zuvandica'' (D.A.Kapan., 1985).<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=Satureja hortensis L. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=http://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:457680-1 |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Plants of the World Online |language=en}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
Summer savory is native in Southeastern Europe and Asia. In Europe, the herb is native in [[Italy]], former [[Yugoslavia]], [[Albania]] and the [[Crimea]]. In Asia, summer savory is native in [[Kazakhstan]], the [[western Himalayas]] and [[Xinjiang]]. The herb has been introduced to North America ([[Canada]], [[Cuba]], [[Dominican Republic]], [[Illinois]], [[New York (state)|New York state]], [[Texas]], [[Vermont]] and [[Wisconsin]]) and to more regions across Europe (the [[Balearic Islands]], [[Belgium]], [[Bulgaria]], [[Corsica]], [[Czech Republic]], [[Denmark]], east and south [[European Russia]], [[France]], [[Greece]], [[Portugal]], [[Romania]], [[Slovenia]], [[Slovakia]], [[Spain]], [[Switzerland]], and [[Ukraine]]) and Asia ([[Bahrain]], [[India]], [[Mongolia]], [[Primorsky Krai|Primorye]] in the [[Russian Far East]], [[Qatar]], the [[United Arab Emirates]], and [[Uzbekistan]]).<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=Satureja hortensis L. |url=https://www.gbif.org/species/2926885 |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=www.gbif.org |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last1=Ravindran |first1=P. N. |chapter=28 - Other herbs and spices: mango ginger to wasabi |date=2012-01-01 |title=Handbook of Herbs and Spices (Second Edition) |pages=557–582 |editor-last=Peter |editor-first=K. V. |series=Woodhead Publishing Series in Food Science, Technology and Nutrition |publisher=Woodhead Publishing |doi=10.1533/9780857095688.557 |isbn=978-0-85709-040-9 |pmc=7152468 |last2=Pillai |first2=G. S. |last3=Divakaran |first3=M.}}</ref> In addition, the herb is doubtfully present in the region of [[South Caucasus]] and [[Turkey]].<ref name=":0" />

== History ==
The Latin name ''Satureja hortensis'' comes from Roman writer [[Pliny the Elder]], and it is said to be a derivative of the word [[satyr]]. Legends state that the herb belonged to this ancient creature, which led to the name satureja.<ref name=":02">{{Cite book |last1=Kowalchik |first1=C. |title=Rodale's illustrated encyclopedia of herbs |last2=Hylton |first2=W.H. |publisher=Emmaus, PA: Rodale Press |year=1998 |pages=452–453}}</ref> Their primary during the [[Ancient Rome|Roman times]] was in cooking. It was used to flavour foods until black pepper made its way to Europe, which replaced most of summer savory's uses.<ref name=":02" /><ref name=":03"/> During the reign of [[Julius Caesar]] the Romans introduced the herb to England, where it also became a popular herb for cooking and was used in medicine. The English name comes from the [[Saxons]] who called it savory for its pungent taste.<ref name=":02" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Burlando |first1=Bruno |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1201/ebk1439812136 |title=Herbal Principles in Cosmetics |last2=Verotta |first2=Luisella |last3=Cornara |first3=Laura |last4=Bottini-Massa |first4=Elisa |date=2010-06-23 |publisher=CRC Press |doi=10.1201/ebk1439812136 |isbn=978-1-4398-1214-3}}</ref> In the 17th century the English botanist [[Nicholas Culpeper|Nicolas Culpeper]] wrote that the herb had wind expelling properties, making summer savory more used in medical purposes. The herb was first cultivated in the 19th century; previously, it was harvested as a wild growing shrub.<ref name=":02" /><ref name="NIPA">{{Cite book |last1=Nybe |first1=E.V. |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.59317/9789389547146 |title=Spices: Vol.05. Horticulture Science Series |last2=Raj |first2=Mini |date=2007-01-15 |publisher=NIPA |doi=10.59317/9789389547146 |isbn=978-93-89547-14-6}}</ref>

In the 21st century, summer savory is cultivated in [[France]], [[Spain]], [[Germany]], [[England]] and other parts of [[Europe]], [[Canada]] and the [[United States|United States of America]]. When bought for culinary use the herb contains both dried leaves and flowers.<ref name="NIPA"/>

== Habitat ==
Summer savory can grow from [[Plant propagation|propagated]] seeds in a moderately fertile environment, usually in a rich, light soil, as they usually take longer to [[Germination|germinate]].<ref name=":03">{{Cite journal |last1=Ejaz |first1=Afaf |last2=Waliat |first2=Sadaf |last3=Arshad |first3=Muhammad Sajid |last4=Khalid |first4=Waseem |last5=Khalid |first5=Muhammad Zubair |last6=Rasul Suleria |first6=Hafiz Ansar |last7=Luca |first7=Marian-Ilie |last8=Mironeasa |first8=Costel |last9=Batariuc |first9=Ana |last10=Ungureanu-Iuga |first10=Mădălina |last11=Coţovanu |first11=Ionica |last12=Mironeasa |first12=Silvia |date=2023 |title=A comprehensive review of summer savory (Satureja hortensis L.): promising ingredient for production of functional foods |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |volume=14 |doi=10.3389/fphar.2023.1198970 |doi-access=free |issn=1663-9812 |pmc=10406440 |pmid=37554989}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cutler |first1=Karan Davis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=NGRyVqNN03EC&q=%22Satureja+hortensis%22&pg=PA328 |title=Herb Gardening For Dummies |last2=Fisher |first2=Kathleen |last3=DeJohn |first3=Suzanne |last4=Association |first4=National Gardening |date=2010-10-29 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-470-88748-6 |pages=328–329 |language=en}}</ref> Usually, this species prefers dry [[gravel]] and stone slopes of up to 1500 meters as their habitat.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Satureja hortensis Summer Savory PFAF Plant Database |url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Satureja+hortensis |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=pfaf.org}}</ref> This herb can be grown in pots, ornamental borders and herb gardens and is an excellent companion plant that can deter [[aphid]]s when grown next to [[Vicia faba|broad beans]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Satureja hortensis |url=https://www.gardenersworld.com/plants/satureja-hortensis/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=BBC Gardeners World Magazine |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Chemical composition ==
The leaves of summer savory are abundant in total [[phenolic compounds]] ([[rosmarinic acid]] and [[flavonoid]]s) that have a powerful antioxidant impact. [[Tannin]]s, [[volatile oils]], [[sterol]]s, [[acid]]s, gums, [[pyrocatechol]], phenolic compounds, and [[mucilage]] are primary components of the Satureja species.<ref name=":03" /> [[Terpene]]s are also another component provided by summer savory that allow its unique taste, smell and health benefits.<ref name="What Is Summer Savory">{{Cite web |title=What Is Summer Savory? |url=https://draxe.com/nutrition/summer-savory/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=Dr. Axe |language=en-US}}</ref> Additionally, it also possesses [[Iron(III) oxide|Fe (III)]] reductive and [[Radical (chemistry)|free radical]] scavenging properties and contains [[mineral]]s like [[potassium]], [[phosphorus]], [[calcium]], [[magnesium]], [[iron]], and [[sodium]], as well as [[vitamin]]s such as [[Vitamin B3|niacin]], [[pyridoxine]], [[riboflavin]], [[thiamine]], [[vitamin A]] and [[vitamin C]]. Its seeds contain chemicals such as [[carvacrol]], [[estragole]] (methyl chavicol), [[caryophyllene]], and [[(E)-caryophyllene|E-caryophyllene]], which are composed of 45% dry basis of fixed oil and 24% protein.<ref name=":03" /><ref name=":12">{{Cite book |last=Nybe |first=E. V. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HHs6ANrJ-MEC&q=%22Satureja+hortensis%22&pg=PA233 |title=Spices |date=2007 |publisher=New India Publishing |isbn=978-81-89422-44-8 |language=en}}</ref> The leaves are a good source of carvacrol, [[Terpinene|γ-terpinene]] and [[Cymene|ρ-Cymene]].<ref name=":03" />

Other than the culinary use as a herb, it can also be extracted for its [[essential oil]]. Leaves yield approximately 0.5-1% essential oil that is light yellow or brown with slightly sharp phenolic notes similar to [[oregano]] and [[thyme]].<ref name=":12" />  Major components of essential oils extracted from summer savory are carvacrol, thymol, γ-terpinene, and ρ-cymene, while α-terpinene, β-caryophyllene and [[Bisabolene|β-bisabolene]] are found in smaller quantities.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hamidpour |first1=Rafie |last2=Hamidpour |first2=Soheila |last3=Hamidpour |first3=Mohsen |last4=Shahlari |first4=Mina |last5=Sohraby |first5=Mahnaz |date=2014-07-01 |title=Summer Savory: From the Selection of Traditional Applications to the Novel Effect in Relief, Prevention, and Treatment of a Number of Serious Illnesses such as Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease, Alzheimer's Disease, and Cancer |journal=Journal of Traditional and Complementary Medicine |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=140–144 |doi=10.4103/2225-4110.136540 |doi-access=free |issn=2225-4110 |pmc=4142450 |pmid=25161917}}</ref>  Phenolic content within the essential oil, especially that of carvacrol, varies from 23.8-55%.<ref name=":12" />

== Ecology ==
Summer savory grows wild but it is also beneficial for the garden ecosystem since it attracts various [[pollinator]]s.<ref name=":04">{{Cite journal |last=Austin |first=Daniel E. |date=1998 |title=The Green Pharmacy |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf02862144 |journal=Economic Botany |volume=52 |issue=3 |pages=266 |doi=10.1007/bf02862144 |s2cid=30891078 |issn=0013-0001|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite book |last=Nybe |first=E. V. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=HHs6ANrJ-MEC&q=summer+savory&pg=PA7 |title=Spices |date=2007 |publisher=New India Publishing |isbn=978-81-89422-44-8 |language=en}}</ref> Because of its tubular flower shape, the [[nectar]] is encapsulated in the flower which makes it hard to reach for pollinators. The main pollinators of summer savory are [[bee]]s, [[bumblebee]]s, [[wasp]]s, [[Bombyliidae]] and [[hoverflies]], which support plant reproduction and seed production. Diaspores are the seeds which are dispersed by ants through a process known as [[myrmecochory]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Düll |first1=Ruprecht |title=Taschenlexikon der Pflanzen Deutschlands und angrenzender Länder: die häufigsten mitteleuropäischen Arten im Porträt |last2=Kutzelnigg |first2=Herfried |date=2011 |publisher=Quelle & Meyer |isbn=978-3-494-01424-1 |edition=7., korrigierte und erw. Aufl |series=Quelle-&-Meyer-Taschenlexikon |location=Wiebelsheim}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Aichele |first1=Dietmar |title=Die Blütenpflanzen Mitteleuropas |last2=Schwegler |first2=Heinz-Werner |date=2000 |publisher=Franckh-Kosmos |isbn=978-3-440-08048-1 |edition=2., überarb. Aufl |location=Stuttgart}}</ref>

The flowers of summer savory are more modest in appearance and, just as with chamomile and thyme, tend to attract a greater number of beneficial insects compared to for example [[rose]]s and [[chrysanthemum]]s that are often favored for their beauty.<ref name=":13">{{Cite book |last1=Association |first1=The National Gardening |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=9WeF9xP6jiEC&q=summer+savory&pg=PR24 |title=Gardening All-in-One For Dummies |last2=Beckstrom |first2=Bob |last3=Cutler |first3=Karan Davis |last4=Fisher |first4=Kathleen |last5=Giroux |first5=Phillip |last6=Glattstein |first6=Judy |last7=MacCaskey |first7=Mike |last8=Marken |first8=Bill |last9=Nardozzi |first9=Charlie |date=2003-02-28 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-7645-2555-1 |language=en}}</ref> This makes it an option for gardeners looking to encourage [[biodiversity]] and provide food for these crucial pollinators while also being easily cultivated from seed or cutting.<ref name=":04" /><ref name=":13" />

The early spring seedlings are often topped for fresh use in June. When the plants are in flower, they may be pulled up and dried for winter use.<ref name=":04" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |last=nchfp |date=2015-01-05 |title=summer savory |url=https://preservingfoodathome.com/tag/summer-savory/ |access-date=2024-01-24 |website=Preserving Food at Home |language=en}}</ref> Summer savory can be collected when the plant reaches around 15 centimetres in height and when it is in full flowering stage. It reaches that point after approximately 75–120 days.<ref name=":4" /> To promote further growth the tops should be regularly trimmed.<ref name=":04" /> For storage, the plant needs to be dried by hanging it up in little bundles.<ref name=":3" /> Once dry, the leaves need to be removed in order to store them in sealed jars and once the seeds brown, they can be preserved with a [[desiccant]] in a similar airtight manner.<ref name=":04" />

The plant only lives for a single summer which makes it an [[annual plant]].<ref name=":04" /><ref>{{Cite web |last=Lea |date=2022-03-31 |title=Savory: growing, care & harvest |url=https://plantura.garden/uk/herbs/savory/savory-overview |access-date=2024-01-24 |website=Plantura |language=en-GB}}</ref>

== Uses ==

=== Cuisine ===
Summer savory is a traditional popular herb in [[Atlantic Canada]], where it is used in the same way [[Common sage|sage]] is elsewhere.<ref name="frontiersin.org">{{Cite journal |last1=Ejaz |first1=Afaf |last2=Waliat |first2=Sadaf |last3=Arshad |first3=Muhammad Sajid |last4=Khalid |first4=Waseem |last5=Khalid |first5=Muhammad Zubair |last6=Rasul Suleria |first6=Hafiz Ansar |last7=Luca |first7=Marian-Ilie |last8=Mironeasa |first8=Costel |last9=Batariuc |first9=Ana |last10=Ungureanu-Iuga |first10=Mădălina |last11=Coţovanu |first11=Ionica |last12=Mironeasa |first12=Silvia |date=2023 |title=A comprehensive review of summer savory (Satureja hortensis L.): promising ingredient for production of functional foods |journal=Frontiers in Pharmacology |volume=14 |doi=10.3389/fphar.2023.1198970 |doi-access=free |pmid=37554989 |pmc=10406440 |issn=1663-9812}}</ref> It is the main flavoring in dressing for many fowl, mixed with ground pork and other basic ingredients to create a thick meat dressing known as ''{{lang|fr|[[cretonnade]]}}'' (''cretonade'') which may be eaten with turkey, goose and duck.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Brown |first=Oliver Phelps |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=u-gDLTTag1oC&dq=Complete+herbalist&pg=PR2 |title=Compelte Herbalist |date=2009 |publisher=Concept Publishing Company |isbn=978-81-7268-190-6 |language=en}}</ref> It also is used to make stews such as [[fricot]], and in potato cakes and meat pies.<ref name="frontiersin.org"/> It is usually available year-round in local grocery stores in dried form and is used in varying proportions, sometimes added to recipes in large spoonfuls (such as in ''{{lang|fr|cretonnade}}''), and sometimes more subtly (as in beans, for which savory has a natural affinity).<ref name="frontiersin.org"/>

Summer savory is a characteristic ingredient of [[herbes de Provence]].<ref name="America">{{Cite web |last=America |first=The Herb Society of |date=2021-07-05 |title=Summer Savory – Herb of the Month |url=https://herbsocietyblog.wordpress.com/2021/07/05/summer-savory-herb-of-the-month/ |access-date=2024-01-23 |website=The Herb Society of America Blog |language=en}}</ref> It is also widely used as a seasoning for grilled meats and barbecues, as well as in stews and sauces.<ref name="frontiersin.org"/>

Summer savory is preferred over [[winter savory]] for use in sausages because of its sweeter, more delicate aroma. It plays an important role in [[Bulgarian cuisine]], providing a strong flavor to a variety of dishes.<ref name="frontiersin.org"/> Instead of salt and pepper, a Bulgarian table will have three condiments: [[salt]], [[Paprika|red sweet pepper]], and summer savory. When these are mixed it is called [[sharena sol]] ({{lang|bg|шарена сол}} 'speckled salt').

Summer savory, known as cimbru, is used in [[Romanian cuisine]], especially in [[sarmale]] (stuffed [[cabbage]] or [[grape leaf]] rolls) and in [[mititei]] (grilled ground meat rolls).<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Cutler |first1=Karan Davis |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=bkz7CAAAQBAJ&dq=Herb+gardening+for+dummies&pg=PA3 |title=Herb Gardening For Dummies |last2=Fisher |first2=Kathleen |last3=DeJohn |first3=Suzanne |last4=Association |first4=National Gardening |date=2010-11-23 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-0-470-61778-6 |language=en}}</ref>

=== Alcohol ===
Regarding its use in alcohol, summer savory is not often used as an ingredient in alcoholic beverages. But with its flavour profile, it is an addition to some artisanal or craft spirits and [[liqueur]]s. The herb, known for its pungent piney flavor with peppery hints, could impart a spicy, peppery note to such beverages, potentially complementing other botanicals since it is often compared to a cross between mint and thyme.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |last=SPICEography |date=2022-10-02 |title=Summer Savory: History, Flavor, Benefits, Uses |url=https://www.spiceography.com/summer-savory/ |access-date=2024-01-16 |website=SPICEography |language=en-US}}</ref><ref name="What Is Summer Savory"/>

Given summer savorys traditional use in [[vinegar]] preservation by the [[Ancient Rome|ancient Romans]], it can be infused in vinegar-based cocktails or used as a garnish to add a subtle, herby touch to certain drinks.<ref name=":04" /> In culinary applications, it is also used because of its ability to add a salty and peppery flavor without increasing [[sodium]] intake.<ref name=":2" />

=== Medicine ===
The use of summer savory dates back to being used by the [[Ancient Rome|Romans]] for traditional medicinal remedies and it has since been used by many other cultures to treat symptoms such as [[cramp]]s, [[Abdominal pain|stomach pains]], [[nausea]], [[indigestion]], and more.<ref name="America"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Bezić |first1=Nada |last2=Šamanić |first2=Ivica |last3=Dunkić |first3=Valerija |last4=Besendorfer |first4=Višnja |last5=Puizina |first5=Jasna |date=March 2009 |title=Essential Oil Composition and Internal Transcribed Spacer (ITS) Sequence Variability of Four South-Croatian Satureja Species (Lamiaceae) |journal=Molecules |language=en |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=925–938 |doi=10.3390/molecules14030925 |doi-access=free |pmid=19255551 |pmc=6253779 |issn=1420-3049}}</ref><ref name="Hamidpour 140–144">{{Cite journal |last1=Hamidpour |first1=Rafie |last2=Hamidpour |first2=Soheila |last3=Hamidpour |first3=Mohsen |last4=Shahlari |first4=Mina |last5=Sohraby |first5=Mahnaz |date=2014-07-01 |title=Summer Savory: From the Selection of Traditional Applications to the Novel Effect in Relief, Prevention, and Treatment of a Number of Serious Illnesses such as Diabetes, Cardiovascular Disease, Alzheimer's Disease, and Cancer |journal=Journal of Traditional and Complementary Medicine |volume=4 |issue=3 |pages=140–144 |doi=10.4103/2225-4110.136540 |doi-access=free |pmid=25161917 |issn=2225-4110|pmc=4142450 }}</ref>

Studies such as “''In Vitro Antibacterial, Antifungal, and Antioxidant Activities of the Essential Oil and Methanol Extracts of Herbal Parts and Callus Cultures of'' Satureja Hortensis ''L.''”  and “''Antispasmodic and Anti-Diarrhoeal Effect of Satureja Hortensis L. Essential Oil.''”, along with others, have proved that there is a relationship between the plant and its curing properties.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Güllüce |first1=M. |last2=Sökmen |first2=M. |last3=Daferera |first3=D. |last4=Ağar |first4=G. |last5=Ozkan |first5=H. |last6=Kartal |first6=N. |last7=Polissiou |first7=M. |last8=Sökmen |first8=A. |last9=Sahin |first9=F. |date=2003-07-02 |title=In vitro antibacterial, antifungal, and antioxidant activities of the essential oil and methanol extracts of herbal parts and callus cultures of Satureja hortensis L |journal=Journal of Agricultural and Food Chemistry |volume=51 |issue=14 |pages=3958–3965 |doi=10.1021/jf0340308 |issn=0021-8561 |pmid=12822930}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Hajhashemi |first1=Valiollah |last2=Sadraei |first2=Hassan |last3=Ghannadi |first3=Ali Reza |last4=Mohseni |first4=Mandana |date=2000-07-01 |title=Antispasmodic and anti-diarrhoeal effect of Satureja hortensis L. essential oil |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378874199002093 |journal=Journal of Ethnopharmacology |volume=71 |issue=1 |pages=187–192 |doi=10.1016/S0378-8741(99)00209-3 |pmid=10904162 |issn=0378-8741|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

These properties are due to the chemical composition and the presence of [[steroid]]s, [[essential oil]]s, [[flavonoid]]s, and other components, which have [[anti-inflammatory]], [[antispasmodic]], [[sedative]], [[antioxidant]], and [[antimicrobial]] properties.<ref name="Hamidpour 140–144"/>
